title: A Nagata ring is universally Japanese (Nagata)
statement: Let $R$ be a Nagata ring [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. Then $R$ is universally Japanese [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]: for every ring map $R\to S$ of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] with $S$ an integral domain, $S$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain], i.e. for every finite extension $L$ of the fraction field of $S$ the integral closure of $S$ in $L$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is a finitely generated $S$-module.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334 (proposition-nagata-universally-japanese), implication (1) => (3), line 46067; its proof uses Lemmas 032O (polynomial-ring-N-2), 032T (quasi-finite-over-nagata), 0333 (characterize-N-1), 032K, 0330 (criterion-analytically-unramified), 032Y, 0331

proof.text: *Transcendental case of (*).* Let $A$ be an integral domain which is a Nagata ring [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring], with field of fractions $K$, and let $B\supseteq A$ be an integral domain generated as an $A$-algebra by one element $x$, with field of fractions $L$; as $A\subseteq B\subseteq L$, the nonzero elements of $A$ are invertible in $L$, so $K\subseteq L$. Suppose $x$ is not algebraic over $K$ [def-weil-algebraic-element]. The evaluation $A[X]\to B$, $X\mapsto x$, from the polynomial ring [def-weil-polynomial-ring] is surjective since $x$ generates $B$, and injective since a nonzero $g\in A[X]\subseteq K[X]$ with $g(x)=0$ would make $x$ algebraic over $K$. So $B\cong A[X]$. The ring $A$ is Noetherian and $A=A/(0)$ with $(0)$ prime, so $A$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain] by the definition of a Nagata ring. By [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-ring-n2] $B\cong A[X]$ is N-2.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334, proof, Step 3 (line 46098), using Lemma Tag 032O (lemma-polynomial-ring-N-2)

proof.text: *Algebraic case of (*): setting up.* Keep $A\subseteq B=A[x]$, $K$, $L$ as in step 1 and suppose $x$ is algebraic over $K$. The subfield $K(x)\subseteq L$ is a finite extension of $K$ [lem-weil-pbc-algebraic-generators-finite-extension]; it contains $A$ and $x$, hence $B$, hence every quotient $b/b'$ of elements of $B$, so $K(x)=L$ and $L/K$ is finite [def-pc-field-extension]. Let $M/L$ be a finite field extension; we must show that the integral closure $S'$ of $B$ in $M$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is a finitely generated $B$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module]. Since $M$ is a finitely generated $L$-module and $L$ a finitely generated $K$-module, $M$ is a finitely generated $K$-module [lem-weil-pbc-finite-module-over-finite-algebra], i.e. $M/K$ is finite. Let $R'\subseteq M$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $M$. As $A$ is N-2 (step 1) and $M/K$ is finite, $R'$ is a finitely generated $A$-module, say generated by $r_1,\dots,r_k$ [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]. By [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-finite-extension-normal] $R'$ is a normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] with field of fractions $M$, and by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-nagata-nagata] (applied to the finite map $A\to R'$) $R'$ is a Nagata ring.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334, proof, Step 4 (line 46110): 'the fraction field of R' is M and R in R' is finite (by the Nagata property of R). This implies that R' is a Nagata ring (Lemma 032T)'

proof.text: *Algebraic case of (*): $S'$ is the integral closure of $T=R'[x]$.* Let $T\subseteq M$ be the subring generated by $R'$ and $x$ (note $x\in B\subseteq L\subseteq M$). Every element of $T$ is a sum $\sum_i\rho_ix^i$ with $\rho_i\in R'$, and writing $\rho_i=\sum_j a_{ij}r_j$ with $a_{ij}\in A$ gives $\sum_i\rho_ix^i=\sum_j(\sum_i a_{ij}x^i)r_j$ with $\sum_ia_{ij}x^i\in B$; so $T$ is the $B$-module generated by $r_1,\dots,r_k$, a finitely generated $B$-module. Its field of fractions is $M$: $R'\subseteq T\subseteq M$ and every element of $M$ is a quotient of elements of $R'$ (step 2). Every element of $R'$ is integral over $A\subseteq B$, hence over $B$ (the same monic equation), so the integral closure $S'$ of $B$ in $M$, a subring of $M$ containing $B$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], contains $R'$ and $x$, hence $T$: $T\subseteq S'$ and $T$ is integral over $B$. Let $T'$ be the integral closure of $T$ in $M$. An element of $S'$ is integral over $B\subseteq T$, hence over $T$: $S'\subseteq T'$. Conversely $T'$ is integral over $T$ and $T$ is integral over $B$, so $T'$ is integral over $B$ [lem-weil-pbc-integral-transitive]: $T'\subseteq S'$. Hence $S'=T'$.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334, proof, Step 4 (line 46110): 'the integral closure S' of S in M is equal to the integral closure of R'[x] in M'; 'To show that S' is finite over S is the same as showing that S' is finite over R'[x]'

proof.text: *Algebraic case of (*): conclusion.* By step 2, $R'$ is a normal domain and a Nagata ring with field of fractions $M$, and $x\in M$; $T=R'[x]\subseteq M$ is the subring generated by $R'$ and $x$. By [lem-weil-pbc-normal-nagata-monogenic-n1] $T$ is N-1 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]: the integral closure $T'$ of $T$ in its field of fractions $M$ (step 3) is a finitely generated $T$-module. By step 3, $T'=S'$ and $T$ is a finitely generated $B$-module, so $S'$ is a finitely generated $B$-module [lem-weil-pbc-finite-module-over-finite-algebra]. As $M/L$ was an arbitrary finite extension, $B$ is N-2. Together with step 1 this proves (*): if $A$ is an integral domain which is a Nagata ring and $A\subseteq B$ is an extension of integral domains with $B$ generated over $A$ by one element, then $B$ is N-2.

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334, proof, Step 4 (line 46110): 'Replace R by R' and S by R'[x] to reduce to (***)', and statement (***) (line 46126)

proof.text: *Claim (M): if $A$ is a Nagata ring and $B$ is an $A$-algebra generated by one element $b$, then $B$ is a Nagata ring.* The $A$-algebra map $A[X]\to B$, $X\mapsto b$, is surjective, so $A\to B$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] and $B$ is Noetherian [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian], [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Let $\mathfrak q\subset B$ be a prime ideal and $\mathfrak p\subset A$ its inverse image, a prime ideal. The quotient map $A\to A/\mathfrak p$ makes $A/\mathfrak p$ a finitely generated $A$-module (generated by $1$), so $A/\mathfrak p$ is a Nagata ring [lem-weil-pbc-finite-over-nagata-nagata], and it is an integral domain. The induced map $A/\mathfrak p\to B/\mathfrak q$ is injective (its kernel is $(\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q))/\mathfrak p=0$), $B/\mathfrak q$ is an integral domain, and it is generated over $A/\mathfrak p$ by the image of $b$. By (*) (step 4) $B/\mathfrak q$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain]. So $B$ is a Nagata ring [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring].

source.place: Algebra, Proposition Tag 0334, proof, Step 2 (line 46090): 'Let q be a prime of S, and let p be the corresponding prime of R. We have to show that S/q is N-2', reducing to (*)

proof.text: *Conclusion.* Let $R$ be a Nagata ring and $R\to S$ a ring map of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] with $S$ an integral domain. Choose generators $s_1,\dots,s_n$ of $S$ as an $R$-algebra; adding the generator $1$ we may assume $n\ge1$. Let $S_i\subseteq S$ be the $R$-subalgebra generated by $s_1,\dots,s_i$, and put $S_0=R$. Then $S_1$ is generated as an $R$-algebra by $s_1$ and $S_{i+1}$ is generated as an $S_i$-algebra by $s_{i+1}$, so by claim (M) of step 5 and induction on $i$ every $S_i$ is a Nagata ring; in particular $S=S_n$ is. Since $S$ is an integral domain, $(0)$ is a prime ideal and $S=S/(0)$ is N-2 [def-weil-pbc-japanese-domain] by the definition of a Nagata ring [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. Hence $R$ is universally Japanese [def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring].
